name: Artificial tears

card.summary: Over-the-counter lubricating eye drops for dry, irritated eyes: standard first-line comfort care, not a whitening or redness fix.
card.aka: Lubricant eye drops, eye lubricants, rewetting drops
card.note: Redness-relief drops containing vasoconstrictors such as tetrahydrozoline are a different product class; a 2023 contamination recall of some brands was linked to serious infections.

quick.overview:
Artificial tears are lubricating eye drops, gels and ointments sold mostly without prescription. They are used for dry eye and for irritation from screens, wind, contact lenses or surgery, and in appearance circles they are discussed as a way to keep the eye surface comfortable and less irritated-looking.

They come with or without preservatives, in thin liquid or thicker gel forms. Reviews and guidance describe them as the usual first step for dry eye, though no single formulation has been shown to be best.
quick.mechanism: They supplement and stabilise the tear film that coats the eye, using water, salts and thickening polymers such as carboxymethylcellulose, hypromellose or hyaluronic acid. They do not contain the living components of natural tears and do not treat the underlying cause of dryness.
quick.risks: Temporary blurred vision is the most common effect, especially with gels and ointments. Preservatives such as benzalkonium chloride can irritate the eye surface with frequent use, which is why preservative-free vials are recommended for heavy use. In 2023 a recall of certain brands followed bacterial contamination linked to eye infections, vision loss and a death. Drops marketed to remove redness contain different active ingredients.

lead: Artificial tears are lubricating eye drops, gels and ointments designed to relieve dryness and irritation of the ocular surface. They are sold mostly over the counter and are used mainly for dry eye disease, for contact lens comfort and during or after some eye procedures [2][4].

For appearance, the chain runs from comfort to look. A dry or irritated eye can appear red, watery, puffy-lidded or tired, and people who care about how their eyes come across use lubricating drops to keep the surface moist and comfortable, particularly during long screen sessions, in dry air, or while wearing contact lenses. Digital eye strain reviews list eye redness, tearing and burning among the commonest symptoms and tie them to a reduced blink rate, which is one reason lubricants are among the most-studied treatments for it [15][16].

Formulations are built from water, electrolytes and thickening polymers such as carboxymethylcellulose, polyvinyl alcohol, hypromellose, hydroxypropyl cellulose, polyethylene glycol or hyaluronic acid. They are made with or without preservatives, and as thin drops for daytime or thicker gels and ointments for longer-lasting but vision-blurring effect [2][1].

A 2023 systematic review of randomised trials (64 articles) reported good evidence that artificial tears improve dry eye symptoms within about a month of regular use, with objective signs taking several months, and that some combination and polyethylene glycol products outperformed some single-ingredient ones [14]. Artificial tears are a different product class from redness-relief drops, which contain vasoconstrictors such as tetrahydrozoline and are marketed for whiter-looking eyes [22].

paras: Dry eye is the most common indication. Dry eye disease is estimated to affect between about 5 and 34 percent of people depending on the population studied, and is more common in women and older adults; contributors include aging, contact lens wear, meibomian gland dysfunction, autoimmune conditions such as Sjogren syndrome, some medications, LASIK and other eye surgeries [13][21][2][1]. Symptoms described by the American Academy of Ophthalmology include stinging or burning, a scratchy or gritty feeling, blurred vision, redness and, paradoxically, watering, which happens as a reflex to dryness [24].

Artificial tears are also used to rewet contact lenses, to lubricate the eye during examinations, and in hospital eye care for people who cannot blink fully, such as some critically ill patients [4][3]. The TFOS DEWS III management report, an international expert review, describes ocular lubricant supplements as the cornerstone of first-line dry eye management, alongside conserving and stimulating tears [12].

Dry or irritated eyes can look red or tired, and appearance-focused communities sometimes mention lubricating drops as a comfort measure for the eye surface. Because screens reduce blinking, the digital eye strain literature is a common route into the topic: Wikipedia cites American Academy of Ophthalmology figures of roughly 5 to 7 blinks a minute during screen use versus about 15 normally, and reviews describe lubricating drops, blinking exercises and environmental changes as the most-studied strain treatments [21][15][16][25].

The research concerns symptoms and tear-film measures, not eye whiteness or other cosmetic outcomes. Redness in a dry eye is one of the listed symptoms, so some users report a less irritated look when dryness is relieved, but no published trial has measured appearance as an endpoint.

Tear film and ocular surface health are also discussed around cosmetic eyelid procedures. A study of upper-eyelid blepharoplasty examined its effects on ocular surface sensation and tear production, and lubricants are among the measures ophthalmologists use for surface dryness in the weeks after eye procedures [26][2].

Most artificial tears combine water and electrolytes with a viscosity agent that helps the film stay on the eye. Common polymers include carboxymethylcellulose (CMC, also called carmellose), hydroxypropyl methylcellulose (hypromellose), polyvinyl alcohol, hydroxypropyl-guar, polyethylene glycol and sodium hyaluronate [2][1][6]. Newer products add lipids or liposomes to support the oily outer layer of the tear film, aimed at evaporative dry eye, and others use hypotonic solutions for aqueous-deficient dry eye [1][14].

Gels and ointments are thicker and longer-lasting but blur vision temporarily; Wikipedia's dry eye article notes that ointments are usually used at bedtime for that reason [2][21]. A related category, autologous serum drops made from a patient's own blood, is used for ocular surface disease under clinical supervision and has been reviewed separately; the TFOS report lists serum and platelet-rich plasma among biologic tear substitutes [5][12].

Artificial tears do not contain the proteins and living components of natural tears and do not treat the cause of dryness. For disease driven by inflammation or blocked meibomian glands, reviews describe other options such as warm compresses, in-office light-based therapies, punctal plugs, and prescription anti-inflammatory drops such as cyclosporine emulsion, which was tested in two multicentre randomised phase 3 trials in 2000 [12][13][24][20].

Preservatives let a multi-dose bottle stay in use without bacterial contamination. Wikipedia lists benzalkonium chloride (BAK), EDTA and chlorobutanol among them, and says high BAK concentrations can be cytotoxic, damage the corneal epithelium and reduce tear and mucin production [2]. The article states that preserved products should be used no more than four to six times a day, and that preservative-free formulations, usually in single-use vials and costing more, are indicated for people who do not tolerate preservatives, who use drops very often or who use several preserved eye drops [2]. The American Academy of Ophthalmology likewise recommends preservative-free versions for use more than six times a day or for people allergic to preservatives [24].

Wikipedia's eye drop article adds that preservatives slow but do not prevent contamination of an opened bottle, and that ophthalmologists commonly advise discarding opened bottles after about three months, while preservative-free drops are sold in single-use containers [23].

sections.h: Variants and how they are compared
paras: Because many products exist, several comparison studies have been run. A 2025 randomised comparison of CMC-, polyethylene glycol 400- and sodium hyaluronate-based lubricants found similar short-term effects on noninvasive tear-film measures, while participants reported better relief with the hyaluronate products [18]. A 2024 randomised trial examined changes in corneal epithelial irregularity after artificial tear treatment [19]. A 2024 non-inferiority trial in China compared a laughter exercise programme with 0.1 percent sodium hyaluronate drops for ocular surface discomfort in dry eye [17].

The 2023 systematic review also noted that results vary between people: not all patients benefit, and if there is no improvement after about a month the authors suggest considering alternative management [14]. A 2016 Cochrane review, as summarised by Wikipedia, found it unclear which over-the-counter formulation works best [2].

sections.h: Redness-relief drops are a different product
paras: Wikipedia is explicit that tetrahydrozoline, the vasoconstrictor in products such as Visine, is not an artificial tear [2]. Tetrahydrozoline (also called tetryzoline) is an alpha-adrenergic agonist that narrows surface blood vessels to relieve redness from minor irritants; it was patented in 1954 and came into medical use in 1959 [22]. Wikipedia describes it as not suitable for prolonged use: its effect fades, and after tolerance develops, stopping can bring redness back or worse (rebound redness) [22]. Eye-drop side effects listed include blurred vision, irritation and dilated pupils [22].

This distinction matters in appearance discussions, because redness-relief drops are marketed for whiter-looking eyes while lubricants are marketed for dryness. Wikipedia's artificial tears article likewise notes that extended use can cause desensitisation [2].

Temporary blurred vision is the most frequently reported effect, especially with gels and ointments. Allergic reactions to ingredients are possible [2]. High concentrations of the preservative benzalkonium chloride have been reported to damage the corneal surface and reduce tear and mucin production, which is why preservative-free options are advised with frequent use [2].

Wikipedia summarises common label guidance: wash hands first, avoid touching the bottle tip to the eye, wait a few minutes between different eye drops, and stop use and seek medical care for allergic reactions such as swelling, itching or breathing difficulty [2]. Mild stinging for a minute or two after any drop is common, and ongoing stinging warrants medical advice [23]. Contact lens wearers are advised to pick products compatible with their lenses [2].

On 2 February 2023, Global Pharma Healthcare recalled artificial tears distributed by EzriCare and Delsam Pharma because of bacterial contamination. A multi-state cluster of drug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections was linked to the drops, with eye infections, permanent vision loss and one death reported [2].

Eye remedies for dryness are described in ancient Egyptian medical texts, according to one encyclopedic account, and saline solutions and later polymer- and lipid-based products followed in the 19th and 20th centuries [1]. Modern research since the 1990s has produced many branded lubricants and comparisons between them, as well as prescription therapies for inflammatory dry eye such as cyclosporine emulsion and, from 2016, lifitegrast [20][21].

Trials of artificial tears are numerous but mostly small and product-specific. An open-label evaluation of a hydroxypropyl-guar gellable lubricant in adults with moderate dry eye assessed signs and symptoms of dryness [6]. Research on tear dynamics has found that tear turnover is reduced in people with symptomatic dry eye, one of the physiological rationales for tear supplementation [7].

Registered studies include small trials of tear osmolarity with sustained use of a branded lubricant [8][9], a trial of two lubricant drops in dry eye disease [10], and a trial of lubricating drops after cataract surgery [11]. The 2023 systematic review of 64 randomised-trial articles is the broadest summary, finding symptom improvement within about a month of regular use and slower sign improvement [14]. The Deutsches Arzteblatt review notes that few randomised controlled therapeutic trials for dry eye had been published as of 2015, and recommends artificial tears for mild symptoms [13].

A meta-analysis of randomised trials compared moisture chambers with lubrication for corneal protection in intensive care patients and noted limited evidence for choosing between them [3]. No published trials were identified that test artificial tears for cosmetic whitening or appearance outcomes.

timeline.event: Ancient Egyptian medical texts describe eye remedies for dry eye, according to one account [1].
Tetrahydrozoline, later the active ingredient of redness-relief drops, is patented; it enters medical use in 1959 [22].
Two multicentre phase 3 trials report on cyclosporine emulsion for moderate to severe dry eye, a prescription alternative to lubricants [20].
An open-label evaluation of a hydroxypropyl-guar gellable lubricant is published in moderate dry eye [6].
A Cochrane review finds no clearly best artificial tear formulation; the FDA approves lifitegrast for dry eye [2][21].
EzriCare and Delsam Pharma artificial tears are recalled after a drug-resistant Pseudomonas outbreak [2].
A systematic review of randomised trials of artificial tears is published in Clinical Optometry [14].
The TFOS DEWS III management report is published, with lubricant supplements as the cornerstone of first-line care [12].

lore.intro: In appearance and eye-care discussion, artificial tears come up as a basic comfort measure for dry, tired or contact-lens eyes, and are often contrasted with redness-relief drops marketed for whiter eyes.

claims.claim: Lubricating drops make eyes look fresher and less tired
claims.believers: People who use drops after screen work or in dry rooms report that eyes feel and look less irritated and scratchy.
claims.experts: Reviews show symptom improvement with regular use in dry eye, and redness is among the listed symptoms; no trial has measured eye appearance directly [14][24].

claims.claim: Artificial tears whiten the eyes the way redness-relief drops do
claims.believers: Some users treat all eye drops as interchangeable for a brighter look.
claims.experts: Wikipedia states that tetrahydrozoline-type redness relievers are not artificial tears; lubricants work on moisture, not on blood-vessel constriction [2][22].

claims.claim: Daily redness-relief drops are a safe cosmetic habit
claims.believers: Users value the quick whitening effect before photos or events.
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes tetrahydrozoline as unsuitable for prolonged use, with effects that fade and possible rebound redness when stopped [22].

claims.claim: Preservative-free drops are better for frequent use
claims.believers: Frequent users prefer single-use vials to avoid irritation from preservatives.
claims.experts: Wikipedia and the American Academy of Ophthalmology both advise preservative-free products for heavy use or preservative sensitivity [2][24].

claims.claim: Long screen sessions dry the eyes, and drops and blinking help
claims.believers: Heavy computer users describe gritty, tired eyes by evening and use drops and breaks.
claims.experts: Reviews tie digital eye strain to reduced blinking and list artificial tears, blinking exercises and environmental changes among the most-studied treatments [15][16].

claims.claim: One brand or ingredient is clearly the best
claims.believers: Users often swear by a particular hyaluronate, gel or lipid product.
claims.experts: A Cochrane review summarised by Wikipedia found it unclear which formulation works best; a 2025 trial found similar tear-film effects across CMC, PEG and hyaluronate, with participants favouring hyaluronate [2][18].

claims.claim: Any bottled eye drop sold in a store is guaranteed sterile
claims.believers: Consumers generally assume store-bought drops are safe.
claims.experts: The 2023 EzriCare and Delsam recall followed a drug-resistant Pseudomonas outbreak with vision loss and a death [2].

angle.goal: Eye comfort and a less irritated look
chain: Lubricant coats and stabilises the tear film
Eyes can look less red, tired or strained
angle.text: People use artificial tears to keep the eye surface moist, so that dryness-related redness, watering and tired-looking eyes are less pronounced, for example after screen work or with contact lenses. They are not marketed as whiteners; the whitening-style products are a separate vasoconstrictor class.
